item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Summary: Supercritical drying is one of the key process decisions that separates a high-porosity aerogel from a heavily shrunken dry gel. For buyers, engineers, and researchers, the important question is not whether a supplier uses the most impressive-sounding process, but whether the chosen drying route consistently delivers the density, pore structure, form factor, and application data the project actually needs.

Aerogel discussions often focus on end properties such as low thermal conductivity, low density, or ultra-high porosity. But those properties do not appear automatically once a wet gel has been synthesized. They depend heavily on what happens during drying. That is why supercritical drying in aerogel manufacturing remains such an important technical and commercial topic.

In simple terms, supercritical drying is a way to remove liquid from a gel without creating the liquid-vapor interface that normally generates capillary forces inside very small pores. Those capillary forces are a major reason ordinary evaporation can shrink, crack, or collapse a fragile gel network. By avoiding that interface, supercritical drying can help preserve the nanostructure that gives aerogels their best-known performance characteristics.

What supercritical drying actually means

According to the IUPAC definition, a supercritical fluid exists above its critical temperature and critical pressure. In aerogel processing, the fluid in the pores is taken into that supercritical region and then removed in a controlled way. Because there is no ordinary liquid-to-gas boundary inside the pore network under those conditions, the drying step can avoid much of the capillary stress that would otherwise deform the structure.

For silica aerogels, carbon dioxide is commonly discussed because its critical point is comparatively accessible. NIST data lists carbon dioxide at roughly 31.0 °C critical temperature and 7.38 MPa critical pressure. In practice, manufacturers usually do not place the original wet gel directly into a CO2 supercritical stage. A solvent-exchange sequence is often required first so the pore liquid is compatible with the drying route.

Why drying is such a decisive step in aerogel manufacturing

A wet gel already contains the basic solid network, but that network is still filled with liquid. If the liquid is removed carelessly, surface-tension effects can pull the structure inward. In conventional evaporation, the smaller the pores and the more delicate the network, the greater the risk of shrinkage, cracking, or loss of porosity.

This is why drying is not just a finishing step. It is one of the main process stages that influences:

  • final density and porosity,
  • dimensional shrinkage,
  • pore-size distribution,
  • thermal insulation performance,
  • optical clarity in some monolithic silica systems,
  • fragility, dusting, and handling behavior,
  • and, at a commercial level, equipment intensity, throughput, and likely cost structure.

That is the main reason supercritical drying became so closely associated with classic silica aerogel production. It is a process route aimed at preserving structure rather than forcing the gel to survive ordinary evaporation.

A typical supercritical drying workflow

The exact manufacturing sequence varies by chemistry and product form, but a simplified aerogel workflow usually looks something like this:

  1. Sol-gel formation: a precursor system forms a wet gel network.
  2. Aging: the network is strengthened or stabilized before drying.
  3. Solvent exchange: the original pore liquid is replaced with a solvent or fluid better suited to later processing.
  4. Supercritical drying: the pore fluid is taken above its critical point and removed under controlled conditions.
  5. Post-processing: the resulting aerogel may be cut, laminated, granulated, reinforced, or converted into blankets, panels, particles, or other forms.

For commercial buyers, that workflow matters because two suppliers can both say they sell “aerogel,” while the actual process controls, reinforcement methods, and final product formats differ significantly.

Why manufacturers still use supercritical drying

Supercritical drying is still relevant because it can be a strong route for preserving fine pore structure and low-density performance in silica-based aerogels. That does not mean it is automatically the best route for every chemistry, part geometry, or price target. It does mean that when a product depends on retaining a very open nanostructure, supercritical drying remains one of the most technically important options.

From an engineering point of view, the value is straightforward: if structure preservation is critical, the drying route must minimize the forces that would otherwise damage that structure. From a business point of view, the value is more nuanced: the process may support premium performance, but it can also imply more specialized equipment and process control.

Supercritical drying vs ambient pressure drying

Ambient pressure drying (APD) is often discussed as an alternative route, especially when manufacturers want to avoid the pressure-vessel severity associated with supercritical systems. APD can be commercially attractive, but it usually requires more careful management of gel chemistry and surface modification so the structure can survive drying without collapsing too far.

In practical terms, the tradeoff is not simply “good” versus “bad.” It is more like this:

  • Supercritical drying is a classic route for structure preservation in delicate porous gels.
  • APD can reduce process severity in some respects, but the formulation and drying strategy often have to work harder to control shrinkage and cracking.

For buyers, the key lesson is that one should not assume all aerogels with similar marketing language were dried the same way or will perform the same way in real service.

Supercritical drying vs freeze drying

Freeze drying is another route sometimes mentioned in porous-material manufacturing. Instead of crossing a normal evaporation pathway, the liquid is frozen and later removed by sublimation. This can also avoid the classic liquid-vapor capillary problem, but it introduces a different set of structural effects. Ice formation and phase behavior can shape pore morphology in ways that are not equivalent to supercritical drying.

That is why freeze drying should be viewed as a different pore-structuring route, not as a universal substitute for supercritical drying. In some polymeric, biobased, or specialized research systems it can be useful. But if the conversation is specifically about high-performance silica aerogels for insulation or transparent monolith-type performance, the manufacturing logic may be quite different.

What this means for insulation buyers and technical sourcing teams

If you are evaluating aerogel blankets, panels, granules, monoliths, or specialty thermal components, it is worth asking a few process-aware questions early:

  • Was the product supercritically dried, ambient-pressure dried, or made by another route?
  • What level of shrinkage control is typical in production?
  • Is the supplied data based on the final commercial form, or only on a laboratory material?
  • How much reinforcement or compositing is built into the product?
  • What mechanical handling limitations should users expect?
  • Is the product optimized for monolith performance, flexible blanket performance, particles, or another format?

These questions matter because the drying route is connected to downstream commercial realities. For example, a process that preserves very high porosity may still require reinforcement or lamination to become field-usable. A product that is easier to scale may come with different density or mechanical tradeoffs. In other words, drying route is not a trivia point. It is part of how application fit is created.

Where supercritical drying shows up most clearly

The relevance of supercritical drying is strongest when the final value proposition depends on preserving a highly open pore network. This is especially important in discussions around silica aerogel materials for:

  • high-performance thermal insulation,
  • lightweight porous monoliths,
  • advanced R&D materials,
  • and certain premium or technically demanding form factors.

At the same time, many commercial buyers never purchase a fragile monolith directly. They buy blankets, composites, or engineered forms that have already been adapted for handling and installation. That is another reason specification teams should ask for data on the exact product form being sold, not only on the base aerogel concept.

A practical way to read supplier claims

When a supplier emphasizes supercritical drying, the claim should be interpreted as a process clue, not as a complete guarantee of quality. It may signal serious attention to pore preservation, but it does not automatically answer questions about batch consistency, reinforcement, installation behavior, or long-term application fit.

A more useful evaluation framework is:

  1. Understand the intended application.
  2. Confirm the product format actually sold.
  3. Review the drying route and any relevant surface-modification or reinforcement approach.
  4. Check technical data generated on the final commercial product.
  5. Compare handling, thickness, installation, and system-integration implications.

For Aerogela readers, that approach is often more valuable than chasing the most advanced-sounding process label. In aerogel markets, manufacturing route and end-use practicality need to be considered together.

Conclusion

Supercritical drying remains one of the most important manufacturing concepts in the aerogel world because it addresses the central challenge of drying a fragile porous gel without destroying the structure that makes the material useful. It is especially important in silica aerogel discussions, where preserved nanostructure is closely tied to low density and strong insulation performance.

But the best commercial question is not simply, “Was it supercritically dried?” The better question is, “Did the overall process produce the specific thermal, structural, mechanical, and form-factor properties this application needs?” That is the level at which buyers, engineers, and R&D teams can make better comparisons between aerogel products and suppliers.

Sources and further reading

  • IUPAC Gold Book: Supercritical fluid
  • NIST Chemistry WebBook: Carbon dioxide critical data
  • Chemical Reviews: Chemistry of Aerogels and Their Applications
  • Gels review: Silica-Based Aerogels in Thermal Insulation of Buildings
  • Britannica: Aerogel overview
  • NASA Glenn: Aerogel overview

item.title: How Aerogel Blankets Are Made: From Sol-Gel Chemistry to Flexible Industrial Insulation
item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Aerogel blankets are among the most widely recognized commercial aerogel products because they translate a laboratory material into a flexible form that can be installed on pipes, vessels, equipment, and building components. For buyers and engineers, however, the finished blanket often hides the complexity of the manufacturing route behind it. Understanding that route matters: process choices influence mechanical robustness, thermal performance, dusting behavior, hydrophobicity, thickness tolerance, and ultimately project economics.

This article provides a practical overview of how silica aerogel blankets are typically produced. It focuses on the industrial process logic rather than proprietary recipes, using conservative, public-source descriptions. Exact chemistries and line configurations vary by manufacturer, but the main steps are consistent across the sector.

Why aerogel blankets matter in the market

Aerogels are highly porous solids derived from a gel in which the liquid phase is removed while preserving much of the nanostructured network. In commercial insulation markets, the most established format is not a fragile monolith but a fiber-reinforced blanket. This product form combines low thermal conductivity associated with silica aerogel with the handling advantages of a fibrous mat.

That combination is important in industrial insulation, energy infrastructure, process plants, offshore systems, and selected building applications. Compared with rigid specialty forms, blankets are easier to cut, wrap, transport, and install in field conditions. For that reason, the blanket format has become the reference point for many real-world aerogel deployments.

The basic manufacturing concept

At a high level, an aerogel blanket is made by creating a silica gel within or around a reinforcing fiber matrix, then removing the pore liquid in a way that preserves the extremely porous structure. The blanket is subsequently treated, dried if needed, converted, and packaged for sale.

Although public descriptions differ in wording, the process can be simplified into five stages:

  • Preparation of a silica sol or precursor system
  • Impregnation of a fiber batting or nonwoven reinforcement
  • Gelation and aging to build a stable porous network
  • Solvent exchange and drying through supercritical or other controlled routes
  • Surface treatment, finishing, quality control, and converting into rolls or sheets

Step 1: Building the silica precursor system

Most commercial aerogel blankets are based on silica chemistry. Public literature commonly describes silica aerogel formation using alkoxide precursors such as tetraethyl orthosilicate or sodium silicate / waterglass-based routes, depending on cost structure and process design. In both cases, the aim is to form a wet gel containing a connected silica network and a liquid-filled pore system.

The precursor chemistry affects several downstream decisions. Alkoxide systems are well known in aerogel research and can yield high-quality networks, while sodium silicate routes can offer cost advantages and have long been studied for larger-scale manufacturing. Industrial producers may also use catalysts, pH control, additives, and tailored solvent systems to steer gel time and pore development.

Why this stage matters for buyers

Even though customers do not usually purchase chemistry, precursor choice can influence consistency, impurity profile, process cost, and scale-up practicality. When a supplier claims a major cost or sustainability advantage, it is often tied in part to this upstream chemistry and solvent management strategy.

Step 2: Impregnating the fiber reinforcement

A standalone silica aerogel monolith is typically too brittle for demanding field installation. To solve that, manufacturers integrate aerogel with a fibrous reinforcement, often a glass fiber mat or similar nonwoven substrate designed to provide flexibility and dimensional stability.

In a common blanket-making approach, the fiber batting is impregnated with the silica sol so that gel formation occurs throughout the porous reinforcement. The goal is not simply to coat the surface, but to distribute silica throughout the internal volume in a controlled way. Uniform impregnation is important because local variations can affect thermal behavior, thickness, dusting, and bend performance.

Manufacturing challenges at this stage include wetting the reinforcement evenly, avoiding large voids, controlling line speed, and keeping the blanket processable before gelation locks the structure in place.

Step 3: Gelation and aging

Once the precursor is in the reinforcement, the sol transitions into a gel. During gelation, a connected silica network forms and spans the blanket structure. The material is still “wet” at this point because the pores remain filled with liquid.

After gelation, the material is usually aged. Aging is a critical but often overlooked step in aerogel manufacturing. Public technical literature describes aging as a means to strengthen the silica network through continued condensation and structural reorganization. Without adequate aging, the network may shrink excessively or crack during later processing.

For industrial blanket production, aging conditions have to balance throughput with network development. Longer or more controlled aging may improve structural integrity, but it also adds time, solvent handling, and cost.

What engineers should infer from this stage

If two blanket products look similar in datasheets, they may still differ in how robustly the aerogel network was developed before drying. This can show up in practical differences such as resilience during handling, performance retention after installation, or behavior under repeated thermal cycling.

Step 4: Solvent exchange and surface modification

Before drying, manufacturers often perform solvent exchange. This replaces the original pore liquid with a fluid more compatible with the drying process. In aerogel science, solvent exchange is important because capillary forces generated during liquid removal can collapse the pore structure if not properly managed.

Manufacturers may also introduce surface modification at this stage, especially to make silica aerogel hydrophobic. Hydrophobic treatment is commercially important because untreated silica can attract moisture, while insulation buyers often want materials that resist liquid water uptake in service conditions. Public descriptions of commercial aerogel blankets frequently emphasize hydrophobicity as a key feature, especially in industrial and building-envelope use cases.

Step 5: Drying without destroying the nanostructure

Drying is the defining technical challenge in aerogel production. If a wet gel is simply evaporated under ordinary conditions, capillary forces can cause major shrinkage or collapse. Aerogel manufacturing therefore uses specialized drying approaches intended to preserve the porous network.

Supercritical drying

Supercritical drying is the classic aerogel route and remains central to many high-performance silica aerogel processes. In this method, the pore liquid is brought above its critical point so there is no liquid-vapor interface creating capillary stress in the conventional sense. Carbon dioxide is widely discussed in public literature as a practical supercritical drying medium after suitable solvent exchange.

From a manufacturing perspective, supercritical drying can help preserve low density and pore structure, but it requires pressure-rated equipment, solvent handling discipline, cycle-time control, and associated capital investment. This is one reason blanket manufacturing know-how can be difficult to replicate at commercial scale.

Ambient-pressure drying and related routes

Not all silica aerogel products rely on the same drying philosophy. Public research and patent literature describe ambient-pressure drying approaches that use surface modification and process control to reduce collapse during solvent removal. These routes are attractive because they may reduce dependence on high-pressure equipment, although tradeoffs can exist in shrinkage management, process complexity, or final material properties.

For buyers evaluating broad aerogel claims, the main point is simple: “aerogel” does not imply a single manufacturing route. Drying technology is one of the major distinctions behind product cost and scale.

Step 6: Finishing, converting, and quality control

After drying, the blanket may undergo trimming, lamination or facing steps, thermal stabilization, dust reduction measures, cutting to thickness or width, and roll conversion for shipment. Manufacturers also perform quality checks covering dimensions, density, thermal conductivity, hydrophobic behavior, and handling characteristics. Depending on the end market, additional testing may include compression behavior, fire-related performance, or resistance to service temperatures.

This finishing stage is commercially significant. A well-made aerogel blanket is not just an aerogel-filled mat; it is a convertable insulation product that must survive packaging, transport, fabrication, and installation while maintaining enough consistency for project specifications.

How process choices affect real-world product differences

For procurement teams, the process overview becomes useful when comparing vendors. Several visible product differences often trace back to manufacturing decisions:

  • Flexibility: influenced by reinforcement architecture, aerogel loading, and drying outcomes
  • Dusting and cleanliness: influenced by network integrity, surface treatment, and finishing
  • Hydrophobicity: influenced by post-treatment chemistry and process control
  • Thickness consistency: influenced by impregnation uniformity and converting quality
  • Cost structure: influenced by precursor route, solvent recovery, drying method, and production scale

That is why buyers should be cautious about treating all aerogel blankets as interchangeable. Similar branding language can mask meaningful process differences.

Questions buyers and engineers should ask suppliers

Most manufacturers will not disclose proprietary recipes, but they should be able to answer process-oriented questions at a useful level. Examples include:

  • Is the product silica aerogel blanket reinforced with glass fiber or another substrate?
  • Is the blanket designed for industrial hot insulation, cryogenic service, building applications, or multiple use cases?
  • Is the product hydrophobic, and how is that verified in quality control?
  • What is the typical product form: rolls, sheets, composites, or faced systems?
  • What certifications or third-party test methods support the thermal and physical claims?
  • How does the supplier manage lot-to-lot consistency at commercial scale?

Further viewing

For readers who want a quick visual refresher on aerogel fundamentals, this YouTube explainer may be useful:

  • Aerogel overview video

Why this topic matters for the aerogel supply chain

Aerogel blankets sit at the intersection of materials science and industrial converting. They are not simply “advanced insulation”; they are engineered composite products whose value depends on repeatable manufacturing. For distributors, OEMs, project engineers, and business development teams, understanding the process helps in three ways: it improves supplier qualification, clarifies application fit, and makes it easier to interpret competing product claims.

It also explains why aerogel blanket production has historically concentrated among a limited number of technically capable manufacturers. Scaling gel chemistry, fiber impregnation, solvent management, drying, and roll goods conversion into a reliable commercial operation is materially harder than making a small aerogel sample in a lab.

Conclusion

The commercial success of aerogel blankets comes from turning a delicate nanoporous material into a flexible insulation product that works in real installations. The path from silica precursor to finished roll involves careful control of gel formation, reinforcement impregnation, aging, solvent exchange, drying, and finishing. Each stage affects product behavior in ways that matter to buyers.

For the aerogel industry, that is the key takeaway: blanket performance is not just about the word “aerogel.” It is about the manufacturing route behind the blanket and the quality discipline used to deliver it at scale.

Sources and further reading

  • Aspen Aerogels — Aerogel Technology
  • Cabot Corporation — Aerogel
  • Aerogel.org — About Aerogel
  • US DOE OSTI — Aerogels Handbook record
  • A Review on the Production of Silica Aerogel and Its Applications

item.title: Aerogel for Acoustic and Noise Control: Where It Helps, Where It Doesn’t, and How to Specify It
item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Aerogel is often introduced as a thermal super-insulator, but that reputation can create confusion when teams start asking whether it is also a high-performance acoustic material. The short answer is: sometimes, but only in the right design context. Aerogel can be relevant for acoustic and noise-control work, yet it should not be marketed as a universal replacement for conventional soundproofing products.

For Aerogela’s audience, the more useful question is not “Is aerogel good for sound?” but “Where can aerogel create acoustic value without overstating what the material can do?” That distinction matters for buyers comparing insulation systems, for engineers designing thin multi-function assemblies, and for business development teams trying to identify credible use cases rather than buzzword-heavy claims.

In practice, aerogel is most interesting for acoustic applications when a project also cares about space savings, weight reduction, thermal control, or a combination of those factors. The strongest case is usually not a bare aerogel monolith by itself. It is an engineered system: a composite, laminated panel, glazing assembly, blanket-based build-up, or another structure where aerogel contributes one part of the final performance package.

Start by separating three different acoustic jobs

Many weak aerogel claims come from mixing together three different goals:

  • Sound absorption — reducing reflections or reverberation by dissipating acoustic energy inside a porous or fibrous structure.
  • Sound transmission loss — blocking sound from passing through a wall, enclosure, window, cover, or panel.
  • Noise and vibration management in lightweight systems — improving overall acoustic behavior in a transport, industrial, or equipment assembly where thickness and mass are constrained.

These are related, but they are not the same design problem. A material that helps absorb mid- to high-frequency sound inside an enclosure may not deliver strong low-frequency barrier performance. A lightweight thermal blanket may help a packaging engineer or industrial OEM, but still fall short of what a heavy, deep, conventional acoustic build-up can do in a building partition. That is why careful specification matters more than generic marketing language.

Why aerogel is acoustically interesting at all

Aerogels attract acoustic interest because of their extremely high porosity, low density, and unusual internal structure. Classic aerogel literature and later work on silica aerogels, composites, and porous systems all point to the same underlying reality: aerogel behaves differently from ordinary dense solids. That makes it worth studying in applications where multifunctionality matters.

From a practical engineering perspective, aerogel can become attractive when a design team wants to combine:

  • thermal insulation,
  • some degree of acoustic control,
  • low weight,
  • limited thickness, and
  • non-traditional form factors such as blankets, flexible laminates, or composite panels.

That is why the conversation is broader than “soundproofing.” In real projects, aerogel may be evaluated because a standard mineral wool, foam, or multilayer acoustic build-up is too thick, too heavy, too thermally conductive, or incompatible with the rest of the system.

Where aerogel can make the most sense

1. Space-constrained thermal-acoustic assemblies

This is one of the most credible commercial angles. If an enclosure, vehicle, battery pack surround, industrial line, or equipment housing needs both thermal protection and some acoustic benefit, aerogel-based layers can be worth studying. The appeal is not necessarily that aerogel beats every acoustic material on a pure decibel basis. The appeal is that it may help deliver a better combined package under tight weight and thickness limits.

For example, a designer may accept moderate acoustic improvement if it comes together with strong thermal insulation and a thinner total assembly. That type of tradeoff is much more realistic than claiming that aerogel alone is a miracle sound barrier.

2. Composite and nonwoven systems

Recent work on aerogel/polymer nonwovens, hybrid porous structures, and other composite architectures is especially relevant. The signal from this literature is consistent: the most promising acoustic results often come from engineered composites, not fragile standalone aerogel pieces. Fiber reinforcement, nonwoven carriers, layered gradients, and controlled pore structures can make the acoustic behavior more useful and more manufacturable.

That matters for buyers because many practical products are not sold as “raw aerogel acoustics.” They are sold as blanket systems, coated fabrics, insulated panels, specialty composites, or envelope/glazing solutions where the aerogel is one performance ingredient within a broader package.

3. Glazing and building-envelope concepts

Aerogel-filled glazing and translucent building systems are another area worth watching. Here, the value proposition is again multi-dimensional: thermal insulation, daylighting or optical behavior, and potentially acoustic benefits at the assembly level. The important phrase is at the assembly level. Window and façade performance depends on the complete build-up: panes, cavities, seals, frame details, facings, and installation quality. Aerogel can contribute, but it does not erase the need for proper system engineering.

For architecture and façade teams, that makes aerogel interesting in niche cases where thermal performance and compact build depth are both important. It does not justify broad claims that aerogel glazing automatically outperforms every conventional high-acoustic window system.

4. Transport and mobile equipment

Aerogel’s low density keeps it on the radar for transportation, aerospace-adjacent systems, and other mobile platforms. In these environments, every millimeter and kilogram can matter. An aerogel-containing acoustic layer may be worth evaluating when the design goal is to manage heat and noise in the same envelope, especially where legacy solutions become too bulky.

Even here, however, the right comparison is usually not “aerogel versus all alternatives.” The real comparison is one engineered multilayer stack-up versus another, each optimized for a different mix of thermal, acoustic, weight, flammability, durability, and processing constraints.

Where expectations should stay modest

Thin sections and low-frequency noise

One of the safest cautions in acoustics is that low-frequency control is hard. Thin porous materials rarely become magical low-frequency blockers just because they are advanced. If a supplier presents very broad “sound insulation” language without specifying thickness, test method, mounting condition, and frequency range, that should trigger more questions.

In many situations, traditional acoustic physics still applies: low-frequency control often needs more mass, more depth, tuned resonant features, or carefully engineered multilayer assemblies. Aerogel may still help inside that system, but it should not be assumed to solve the hardest part by itself.

Confusing thermal performance with acoustic performance

This is another recurring mistake. A strong thermal-insulation story does not automatically imply equally strong acoustic behavior. Thermal conductivity, pore-scale heat transport, and sound attenuation are related only indirectly. A material can be outstanding for thermal insulation and still need substantial engineering work before it becomes a competitive acoustic solution in a given format.

Mechanical fragility and cost realism

Many aerogel systems also come with handling, durability, or cost constraints. Those issues do not make the technology irrelevant, but they do affect where it fits. In projects where standard acoustic materials already work well and thickness is available, aerogel may simply be unnecessary. The strongest use cases tend to be the ones where conventional options run into thermal, space, or weight limitations.

What buyers and engineers should ask suppliers

If an aerogel-based product is presented for acoustic or noise-control use, a practical technical review should include questions such as:

  • Was the result measured on the raw material or on the final assembly?
  • Which acoustic metric was reported? Sound absorption coefficient, transmission loss, STC-style rating, insertion loss, or something else?
  • What frequency range improved? Broadband claims without frequency detail are weak.
  • What was the total thickness and areal density? Performance should be judged relative to geometry and mass.
  • What was the mounting or backing condition? Acoustic results can shift dramatically depending on installation.
  • Is the product optimized for thermal insulation, acoustic control, or a compromise between both?

These questions help separate real engineering value from generic advanced-materials branding.

How Aerogela readers should interpret the current landscape

The evidence base around aerogel acoustics is promising, but uneven. There is credible foundational work on the acoustic behavior of silica aerogels, meaningful research on aerogel-containing composites and nonwovens, and useful assembly-level studies in glazing and multifunctional insulation systems. At the same time, a lot of the published signal remains lab-scale, highly formulation-specific, or difficult to compare across different test methods.

That means the right market stance is neither dismissal nor hype. Aerogel does have a place in acoustic and noise-control discussions, especially where a system needs to do more than one job at once. But the most defensible commercial messaging is narrow and specific: aerogel can be a valuable enabler in lightweight, multifunctional, or space-limited acoustic assemblies. That is a much stronger position than calling it a universal soundproofing answer.

Practical takeaway

For most projects, aerogel should be evaluated as part of a system architecture rather than as a standalone acoustic miracle material. When the project is driven by thin build depth, thermal-plus-acoustic requirements, or aggressive weight targets, aerogel becomes much more compelling. When the job is simply to add economical sound control and thickness is available, conventional acoustic materials may still be the more straightforward choice.

In other words, aerogel is often most valuable when the design problem is constrained and multi-objective. That is exactly why it remains strategically important for advanced insulation, specialty transportation, and next-generation envelope concepts.

Selected sources and further reading

  • Hüsing & Schubert, Aerogels—Airy Materials: Chemistry, Structure, and Properties
  • Pierre & Pajonk, Chemistry of Aerogels and Their Applications
  • Gross et al., Acoustic properties and potential applications of silica aerogels
  • Acoustic and thermal properties of silica aerogels and xerogels
  • Experimental performance evaluation of aerogel glazing systems
  • Investigation on sound absorption properties of aerogel/polymer nonwovens

item.title: Aerogel in Spacecraft and Mars Missions: What Real NASA Use Cases Teach Engineers and Buyers
item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Aerogel is often described in broad terms as a “space-age insulation,” but that phrase is not very helpful for engineers, buyers, or business development teams trying to understand what real aerospace use cases actually prove. The better question is this: when NASA or JPL selected aerogel for a mission, what problem was the material solving inside the system?

That question matters because aerospace material selection is rarely driven by novelty alone. Spacecraft hardware is constrained by mass budget, thermal leakage, geometry, contamination risk, mechanical handling, and mission reliability. A material can be scientifically impressive and still be a poor choice if it does not solve a specific engineering bottleneck. In the strongest public NASA case studies, aerogel was not used because it sounded advanced. It was used because a conventional alternative would have added too much weight, lost too much heat, or damaged the target sample.

For Aerogela’s audience, the practical value is not just historical curiosity. Spaceflight examples can help terrestrial engineers and sourcing teams understand where aerogel is genuinely differentiated: highly constrained thermal paths, low-mass functional systems, and situations where “good enough” conventional insulation becomes too bulky or too heavy.

Why aerospace teams keep revisiting aerogel

NASA’s public mission and materials pages repeatedly point to two core reasons aerogel attracts aerospace attention: very low density and unusually strong thermal-insulation performance for its weight. Those two attributes are easy to state, but the real significance appears only when a mission architecture is under pressure.

In aerospace systems, every extra gram can affect launch cost, packaging, deployment, mobility, or available payload margin. At the same time, heat loss can directly affect power consumption, instrument stability, survival margins, and system design complexity. That combination is why aerogel continues to matter. It is not automatically the best material everywhere, but it becomes strategically interesting when engineers need to conserve both thermal energy and mass.

Just as important, NASA’s better-known aerogel examples show that the material is not tied to a single job. In one mission, aerogel may be chosen because it slows particles gently enough to preserve them. In another, it may be used because it reduces heat leakage through an awkward instrument pathway. The lesson is simple: aerogel should be evaluated by function and system constraints, not by generic marketing language.

Case study 1: Mars Exploration Rover Mini-TES and the problem of thermal leakage

One of the most useful Mars-specific examples comes from the Mars Exploration Rover mission. Official mission material for the Mini-TES instrument described it as being mounted inside the rover’s warm electronics box while looking outward through a periscope assembly. That configuration created a classic engineering problem: the instrument needed an external optical path, but external paths also create opportunities for heat loss.

According to the mission description, the Mini-TES instrument was surrounded by aerogel insulation to minimize heat loss through that periscope arrangement. That is an extremely important point because it shows a realistic, non-hype aerospace use case. Aerogel was not being promoted as a decorative “future material.” It was being used to manage a narrow, thermally sensitive interface in a cold operating environment.

The broader lesson for engineers is that aerogel becomes compelling when thermal leakage happens through geometry that is difficult to insulate with ordinary bulk materials. Penetrations, sensor paths, optical interfaces, feedthroughs, and compact housings can all create weak points in a thermal system. In those locations, the design team may not have enough room for thick conventional insulation, and added mass may also be undesirable. Aerogel’s role, in that context, is not abstract. It is targeted thermal control.

This is also a good reminder that “Mars use case” does not mean the entire rover was simply wrapped in aerogel. The more defensible story is narrower and better: aerogel helped solve a specific instrument-level thermal-management problem where space, heat flow, and mission conditions were all tightly constrained.

What the Mars example teaches terrestrial buyers

For non-space applications, the Mini-TES example translates surprisingly well. Many industrial systems have the same kind of bottleneck even if the environment is less extreme than Mars. Examples include:

  • instrument enclosures with viewing ports or probe passages,
  • battery or electronics assemblies where heat-sensitive sections sit near constrained interfaces,
  • compact insulated housings where every millimeter of thickness matters,
  • process equipment with difficult penetrations or access points, and
  • specialized mobility systems where insulation performance has to be balanced against weight.

In all of these cases, a buyer should not ask only for the lowest thermal conductivity number on a datasheet. The more useful question is whether aerogel reduces system-level penalties that other materials create. Does it save thickness? Reduce heat leak at a problematic interface? Lower weight while preserving thermal performance? Simplify a design that would otherwise need a bulkier thermal build-up? Those are the kinds of decisions aerospace case studies help clarify.

Case study 2: Stardust and aerogel as a low-density capture medium

The Stardust mission demonstrates a very different but equally important lesson. Official NASA and JPL mission descriptions explain that Stardust collected cometary and interstellar dust in aerogel, using the material as a low-density medium to “soft-catch” and preserve high-speed particles.

This is not a thermal-insulation story, but it is highly relevant to how advanced materials should be evaluated. Stardust did not use aerogel because the material had a fashionable reputation. It used aerogel because the mission needed a way to capture tiny fast-moving particles while minimizing destructive impact effects. In other words, the selected property was ultra-low-density functional behavior, not simply thermal resistance.

That matters because it highlights one of the most useful mindset shifts for Aerogela readers: aerogel is a platform material family, not a one-line value proposition. In practical markets, buyers often see aerogel discussed only through industrial insulation or blanket products. Those are commercially important formats, but the spacecraft example reminds us that the real selection logic begins with mission function. What interaction must the material support? What failure mode is it preventing? What penalty is it reducing?

For Stardust, the answer was sample preservation under extreme capture conditions. For Mars Mini-TES, the answer was heat-loss control through a constrained instrument path. Same material family, different engineering logic.

The common thread across both missions

At first glance, Mars thermal insulation and comet-dust capture seem unrelated. But together they reveal a consistent selection pattern. Aerogel becomes attractive when a design team faces an awkward tradeoff that conventional materials handle poorly.

In one case, the problem is thermal leakage through a geometry that must remain functional. In the other, the problem is capturing fragile particles without excessive damage while staying within spacecraft mass limits. The common thread is not “aerogel is amazing.” The common thread is that aerogel can outperform more ordinary options when the system asks for low mass plus highly specialized performance.

That is a better commercial lesson than generic claims about space heritage. If a supplier says a product is “used in aerospace,” a serious buyer should still ask what function the aerogel was performing in that application. Was it reducing heat flow? Protecting a payload? Enabling particle capture? Supporting a lightweight composite concept? The answer matters far more than the prestige of the sector alone.

Where buyers should be careful not to over-read space heritage

Aerospace examples are valuable, but they can also be misused in marketing. A few cautions are worth keeping in mind.

1. Mission success does not mean a direct one-to-one industrial substitute

A material that works in a spacecraft subsystem may still be too expensive, too fragile, too processing-intensive, or too specialized for a standard industrial installation. Space heritage is a credibility signal, not an automatic commercial fit.

2. System design matters as much as material property

In the Mini-TES example, the key value was not simply a low conductivity number in isolation. It was the ability to manage heat flow in a specific assembly. Likewise, Stardust was not “saved by aerogel alone.” The collector architecture, mission geometry, and overall spacecraft design all mattered.

3. Functional claims should stay narrow

Real mission use cases support precise claims better than broad ones. It is safer to say aerogel helped reduce heat loss through a rover instrument pathway than to imply all Mars rover thermal problems were solved by aerogel. It is safer to say aerogel enabled soft capture of cometary particles than to generalize that every ultra-lightweight aerospace barrier should be made from aerogel.

A practical screening framework for engineers and sourcing teams

If you are evaluating aerogel for a demanding application, the aerospace examples suggest a useful screening framework:

  • Identify the exact bottleneck. Is the problem thermal leakage, thickness, weight, sample protection, acoustic/thermal multifunctionality, or something else?
  • Locate the constrained geometry. Aerogel is often most valuable where space is limited or interfaces are awkward.
  • Compare on system penalty, not just material property. Ask what mass, thickness, or energy penalties conventional options impose.
  • Check integration realities. Handling, durability, dusting, facing materials, encapsulation, and assembly method may matter as much as the core aerogel itself.
  • Demand application-specific evidence. “Used in space” is less useful than data, test conditions, and configuration details relevant to your design.

This is the difference between buying an advanced material because it sounds impressive and selecting one because it solves a high-cost design compromise.

Conclusion: the best aerogel stories are specific

NASA’s most useful aerogel examples do not support hype. They support specificity. On the Mars Exploration Rover Mini-TES instrument, aerogel helped reduce heat loss in a constrained thermal pathway. On Stardust, aerogel helped capture fast-moving particles gently enough to preserve them for return to Earth. In both cases, the material mattered because the engineering problem was difficult, not because the word “aerogel” carried prestige.

For Aerogela readers, that is the real takeaway. The strongest aerogel opportunities usually appear where a design has an expensive compromise: too much heat loss, too much mass, too little space, or too much risk of damaging what the system is trying to protect. When that compromise is real, aerogel can become more than an interesting material. It can become the practical answer to a problem other options handle poorly.

Selected sources and further reading

  • NASA Science — Stardust mission overview
  • NASA JPL — Stardust mission page (readable mirror)
  • NASA Science — Mars Exploration Rovers: Spirit and Opportunity
  • NASA Mars Exploration Rover science instruments page (Mini-TES link now redirects to the current NASA Science instrument overview)

item.title: Aerogel in EV Battery Thermal Runaway Protection: What Engineers and Sourcing Teams Need to Know
item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Electric vehicle battery safety has become one of the defining engineering challenges of the current decade. As cell energy densities climb past 250–300 Wh/kg and packs push beyond 800V architectures, the margin between normal operation and thermal runaway narrows. For engineers and sourcing teams evaluating thermal barrier materials, aerogel is no longer a laboratory curiosity — it is an increasingly specified component in production EV battery packs. This article looks at what real testing and deployment data actually show, where aerogel fits in the thermal barrier stack, and how to evaluate it against alternatives.

What Thermal Runaway Propagation Actually Means for Pack Design

Thermal runaway in a single lithium-ion cell is difficult to prevent entirely. Internal short circuits caused by manufacturing defects, mechanical damage, or electrode degradation can push a cell past its stability threshold, releasing stored chemical energy as heat that can exceed 700°C. The real engineering problem is not stopping that first cell — it is preventing the failure from propagating to adjacent cells.

When one cell enters thermal runaway, it ejects hot gases, flames, and conductive debris toward neighboring cells. If those neighbors absorb enough heat to cross their own thermal runaway threshold, a cascading failure spreads through the pack. In a dense prismatic or pouch cell layout with minimal inter-cell spacing, propagation can move through an entire module in seconds.

This is where thermal barrier materials come in. Inserted between cells or wrapped around modules, these materials must accomplish several things simultaneously: delay heat transfer to adjacent cells, resist flame and hot gas impingement, maintain mechanical integrity under cell swelling, and do all of this within tight thickness and weight budgets that directly affect pack energy density.

Why Aerogel's Physical Structure Makes It Effective

Silica aerogel's thermal insulation performance comes from its nanoporous microstructure, not from any exotic chemistry. The material is typically 90–99% air by volume, with pore diameters in the 2–50 nanometer range. Three heat-transfer mechanisms are suppressed simultaneously:

  • Solid conduction is minimized because very little solid silica exists in the cross-section. The tortuous, fractal-like solid network creates an extremely long effective path for conductive heat transfer compared to a dense material.
  • Gas-phase convection and conduction are suppressed through the Knudsen effect. When pore diameters are smaller than the mean free path of gas molecules (approximately 70 nm for air at standard conditions), gas molecules collide with pore walls more frequently than with each other. This dramatically reduces the ability of gas to transport heat through the material.
  • Radiative heat transfer is scattered and absorbed by the aerogel matrix. For high-temperature applications, opacifiers such as carbon black or titanium dioxide are added to further block infrared radiation.

The result is a material with thermal conductivity in the range of 0.013–0.018 W/m·K at ambient temperature — substantially lower than alternatives like mica sheets (0.5–0.8 W/m·K), ceramic fiber blankets (0.05–0.12 W/m·K), or intumescent coatings. For battery applications, this means aerogel can achieve equivalent thermal delay in a fraction of the thickness, which translates directly into more space for active cell material and higher pack-level energy density.

Key Material Properties for Battery Barrier Specifications

When evaluating aerogel for EV battery thermal barriers, several properties beyond thermal conductivity matter in practice:

Thickness and packing efficiency

Production EV applications typically use aerogel pads in the 1–6 mm thickness range, with 2–3 mm being common for prismatic cell barriers. Every millimeter of inter-cell material reduces the space available for electrodes and electrolyte, so the material's insulation per unit thickness is the critical figure of merit. Aerogel's low thermal conductivity means a 2 mm pad can provide thermal delay comparable to 40–80 mm of mica — a difference that directly impacts pack energy density.

Compression behavior

Cells expand and contract during charge-discharge cycles. Pouch cells in particular can swell by several percent over their lifetime. Thermal barrier materials must accommodate this cyclic compression without losing insulating performance or suffering permanent deformation. Aerogel composites (aerogel combined with fiber blankets) offer better compressive recovery than monolithic silica aerogel, which is inherently brittle. Typical compressive strength values for commercial battery-grade aerogel pads range from 0.07 to 0.7 MPa (10–100 psi) depending on formulation and density.

Fire resistance and thermal stability

Silica aerogel is inherently non-combustible — silica does not burn and melts at approximately 1,700°C. Commercial aerogel composites for battery applications typically withstand direct flame exposure at 1,000–1,200°C for 15–30 minutes depending on thickness. This is critical during a thermal runaway event where cell venting can produce sustained flame impingement on adjacent cells. Many commercial products achieve Class A fire ratings and UL 94 V-0 classification.

Electrical insulation

Silica aerogel provides dielectric strength of approximately 10–20 kV/mm, making it an effective electrical insulator between cells — an important secondary function, since conductive debris ejected during thermal runaway could otherwise create short circuits across neighboring cells.

Real-World Deployment: What Is Confirmed

The most clearly documented case of aerogel in a production EV platform is the partnership between Aspen Aerogels (NYSE: ASGN) and General Motors. Aspen announced a multi-year supply agreement with GM in 2022 for aerogel thermal barriers on the Ultium battery platform, which underpins vehicles including the Chevrolet Blazer EV, Cadillac Lyriq, and GMC Hummer EV. This partnership is documented in Aspen's SEC filings and public press releases from both companies, making it the highest-confidence public example of aerogel in series production EVs.

Beyond GM, the picture becomes less transparent. Industry reporting suggests that several major battery manufacturers — including Samsung SDI and CATL — have evaluated or adopted aerogel barriers for prismatic and pouch cell designs, but specific OEM-level applications are typically covered by nondisclosure agreements. Chinese EV makers including NIO, XPeng, and Li Auto have been reported by trade publications to incorporate aerogel in some models, driven by the mandatory GB 38031-2020 safety standard. However, detailed confirmation of which specific vehicle models and cell formats use aerogel, and at what thickness, is rarely available publicly.

This information asymmetry is important for sourcing teams to understand: the aerogel supply chain for automotive batteries is real and growing, but much of the deployment detail remains proprietary. Verification at the component level often requires teardown analysis or direct engagement with Tier 1 suppliers.

Regulatory Drivers That Are Accelerating Adoption

Three regulatory frameworks are directly relevant to aerogel adoption in EV battery packs:

GB 38031-2020 (China — mandatory)

China's GB 38031-2020 standard, effective since January 2021, requires that thermal runaway in a single cell shall not cause fire or explosion in the battery pack within five minutes — providing occupant escape time — or that propagation to other cells be prevented entirely. Test methods include initiating thermal runaway via heating, nail penetration, or overcharge. This standard applies to all EVs sold in China, the world's largest EV market, and is a primary driver of aerogel demand from Chinese battery manufacturers.

UN ECE R100 Revision 3 (EU and international)

The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Regulation No. 100, Revision 3, introduces thermal propagation test requirements being phased in across the EU from 2023 through 2025. The regulation requires that vehicles provide at least five minutes of warning before a hazardous situation develops outside the battery pack following a thermal runaway event. This aligns with the Chinese approach and is driving European OEMs and battery makers to evaluate enhanced thermal barriers.

SAE J2464 (USA — voluntary)

SAE J2464 provides test procedures for EV battery abuse testing, including mechanical (crush, penetration), thermal (external heating), and electrical (overcharge, short circuit) abuse scenarios. While not a pass-fail mandate, it is widely referenced by US OEMs and provides the test methodology framework that many manufacturers use internally. There is no current US federal requirement equivalent to GB 38031 or ECE R100 for thermal propagation specifically, though NHTSA has been evaluating rulemaking in this area.

The common thread across all three frameworks: regulators are moving from "survive a single-cell event" toward "contain the event and protect occupants." This regulatory trajectory favors high-performance thermal barriers and is one reason aerogel demand from the automotive sector is growing faster than overall aerogel market growth.

Key Suppliers in the EV Battery Aerogel Space

The supplier landscape for battery-grade aerogel is concentrated but expanding:

  • Aspen Aerogels (USA) is the most visible supplier to the automotive sector, with the GM Ultium partnership and reported supply agreements with other major OEMs. Their product lines include thin aerogel blankets specifically engineered for battery thermal barriers.
  • JIOS Aerogel (Singapore/South Korea) targets the Asian EV battery market with aerogel blankets and silicone-aerogel composite products. The company has reported collaborations with Asian battery manufacturers.
  • Chinese producers including Guangdong Alison (Sino-Aerogel), Nano High-Tech, Huaqing New Material, and several others are competing in the domestic market. China's mandatory thermal propagation standard has created strong domestic demand that multiple domestic suppliers are addressing.
  • Cabot Corporation (USA) supplies aerogel particles (LunaQ, Nanogel product lines) that can be incorporated into composite thermal barrier products, though they serve more as a materials supplier than a finished-product manufacturer for this application.
  • European suppliers including Active Aerogels (Portugal), Enersens (France), and Svenska Aerogel (Sweden) are developing or offering products targeting the EV sector, though their automotive market presence is currently smaller than Aspen's or the major Chinese producers.

Aerogel vs. Alternative Thermal Barrier Materials

Aerogel competes against several established materials in the battery thermal barrier space. Understanding the trade-offs is essential for specifying engineers:

Mica sheets are the most common incumbent. They offer excellent electrical insulation and fire resistance at low cost. However, mica's thermal conductivity (0.5–0.8 W/m·K) is 30–60 times higher than aerogel's, meaning equivalent thermal delay requires much greater thickness. Mica is also rigid and brittle, making it harder to accommodate cell swelling and module tolerances.

Ceramic fiber blankets provide moderate thermal insulation (0.05–0.12 W/m·K) and good flexibility, but they are thicker than aerogel for equivalent performance and can shed fibers that create contamination concerns in clean battery assembly environments.

Intumescent coatings expand when heated to form an insulating char layer. They are thin at room temperature and relatively inexpensive, but their activation is irreversible — once triggered, the coating expands permanently. They also provide limited thermal delay compared to aerogel's continuous insulation.

Phase change materials (PCMs) absorb heat during the solid-to-liquid transition, providing temporary thermal buffering. However, their capacity is finite — once the phase change is complete, thermal protection drops substantially. PCMs are typically used as a complement to passive barriers, not a replacement.

In practice, many pack designs use layered approaches combining these materials. Aerogel is increasingly specified as the primary thermal barrier layer where space is tightest and performance requirements are highest, with mica or ceramic materials used in less space-constrained regions.

Practical Considerations for Engineers and Sourcing Teams

  1. Specify thermal delay time, not just thermal conductivity. The relevant metric is how many seconds or minutes the barrier material delays peak temperature rise on the protected side of the barrier during a simulated thermal runaway event. This depends on thickness, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, and the specific test protocol.
  2. Account for compression in service. Request test data for thermal performance under compressive loads representative of your cell format and module design. Aerogel's thermal conductivity increases modestly under compression, and long-term creep can reduce thickness over the pack's design life.
  3. Verify fire resistance under realistic conditions. Standard fire ratings (UL 94, Class A) are a starting point, but battery thermal runaway produces a specific combination of flame, hot gas, and particulate ejecta. Request or conduct testing that simulates actual cell venting conditions, not just a standard flame exposure.
  4. Evaluate total cost of ownership, not per-kilogram material cost. Aerogel is more expensive per kilogram than mica, but its superior insulation per unit thickness can enable higher pack energy density (more cells in the same volume), which has significant system-level value. The cost comparison should be done at the pack level, not the material level.
  5. Qualify multiple suppliers. The aerogel supply chain for automotive batteries is still consolidating. Production capacity, quality consistency, and delivery reliability vary significantly between suppliers. For production programs, dual-sourcing is prudent.

Conclusion

Aerogel is transitioning from a high-performance niche material to a mainstream component in EV battery safety systems, driven by tightening thermal propagation regulations and the performance demands of high-energy-density cell designs. The physics are straightforward: nanoporous silica provides thermal insulation per unit thickness that no competing material can match, and this matters when every millimeter of inter-cell space directly reduces pack energy density.

For engineers and sourcing professionals evaluating thermal barrier options, the practical path forward is to specify system-level requirements (thermal delay time, compression resistance, fire endurance), test under realistic conditions, and compare materials on total pack-level impact rather than per-kilogram cost. The confirmed deployment in GM's Ultium platform and the strong pull from China's GB 38031 standard suggest that aerogel's role in battery safety will continue to expand as EV production scales and regulatory requirements tighten globally.

Selected Sources and Further Reading

  • Aspen Aerogels — investor presentations and SEC filings documenting GM supply agreement and EV product lines
  • GB 38031-2020 — China's "Electric Vehicles Safety Requirements" standard (mandatory for all EVs sold in China)
  • UNECE Regulation No. 100, Revision 3 — thermal propagation requirements for the EU and international markets
  • SAE J2464 — "EV and HEV RESS Abuse Testing" standard
  • JIOS Aerogel — company publications on aerogel for battery thermal management

item.title: Leading Aerogel Research Centers Worldwide: Where Innovation Meets Industry
item.dc:creator: aerogelaadmin
item.content:encoded:
Aerogel research is no longer confined to a handful of specialist laboratories. Today, a global network of national labs, university groups, and applied research centers is pushing the boundaries of what aerogel materials can do — from ultra-light graphene structures and 3D-printed aerogel components to biopolymer aerogels made from cellulose and alginate. For engineers, sourcing teams, and business development professionals working in the aerogel industry, knowing where the cutting-edge work is happening can inform partnerships, technology scouting, and product development decisions.

This article surveys leading aerogel R&D institutions across three continents, highlights what makes each group distinctive, and explains how industry professionals can benefit from understanding the research landscape.

United States: National Laboratories Driving Aerogel Innovation

NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — Pasadena, California

NASA JPL holds a unique place in aerogel history. The laboratory developed the silica aerogel tiles used on the Stardust mission (launched 1999) to capture cometary and interstellar dust particles at speeds exceeding 6 km/s. The aerogel "tennis racket" collector successfully trapped particles from Comet Wild 2 in 2004, and the samples were returned to Earth for analysis in 2006. This remains one of the most iconic real-world applications of silica aerogel.

Beyond Stardust, JPL continues to develop aerogel-based thermal insulation for spacecraft, Mars rovers, and deep-space instruments. NASA's technology transfer programs have also licensed aerogel manufacturing methods to commercial entities, directly seeding the terrestrial insulation industry. For sourcing teams, JPL's published technical reports on aerogel durability, outgassing, and thermal performance in vacuum environments remain valuable reference documents.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) — Oak Ridge, Tennessee

ORNL has built a broad aerogel research portfolio spanning carbon aerogels, graphene aerogels, and silica aerogels. Key focus areas include high-surface-area carbon aerogels for supercapacitor and battery electrodes, graphene aerogel structures for thermal management, and water purification membranes incorporating aerogel materials.

One of ORNL's practically significant contributions is research on ambient-pressure drying techniques — methods that eliminate the need for supercritical CO₂ drying, which is one of the main cost drivers in aerogel manufacturing. Published work from ORNL in journals such as Carbon, Advanced Materials, and ACS Nano provides a knowledge base for manufacturers looking to reduce production costs.

ORNL collaborates with DOE-funded initiatives and licenses technology through UT-Battelle, making it an important node for companies exploring next-generation aerogel materials.

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) — Livermore, California

LLNL is at the forefront of additive manufacturing for aerogels. The laboratory pioneered direct ink writing (DIW) techniques for 3D-printing graphene and polymer aerogels into complex geometries that are impossible to achieve with conventional sol-gel casting. This work, published in Nature Communications and Advanced Materials, opens possibilities for custom-shaped aerogel components in thermal management, energy storage, and catalysis.

LLNL also develops ultra-low-density aerogel target materials for the National Ignition Facility (NIF), where aerogels serve as precision components in high-energy-density physics experiments. These extreme-performance applications push the boundaries of aerogel density, uniformity, and mechanical integrity.

Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) — Richland, Washington

PNNL focuses on aerogels for building energy efficiency and environmental remediation. Research areas include aerogel-based coatings and composites for building envelope applications, as well as improved ambient-drying methods for silica aerogel production. For building insulation manufacturers, PNNL's published data on aerogel thermal performance in realistic wall assemblies is a practical resource.

China: CAS Institutes and University Partnerships

CAS Suzhou Institute of Nano-Tech and Nano-Bionics (SINANO)

Located in Suzhou, Jiangsu Province, SINANO is one of the most active CAS institutes for aerogel research. The institute's work spans silica aerogels, carbon aerogels, and nanocomposite aerogels, with particular emphasis on ambient-pressure drying methods and cost-effective production techniques. SINANO has also published on flexible aerogel blankets and aerogel-based adsorbents for water treatment.

SINANO collaborates with Chinese aerogel manufacturers for technology transfer, making it a key bridge between academic research and commercial production in China's rapidly growing aerogel market.

CAS Institute of Metal Research (IMR) — Shenyang

The Institute of Metal Research in Shenyang has published on ultra-light graphene aerogels with record-low densities, contributing to the broader field of lightweight carbon materials for energy storage and catalysis. IMR's work on graphene aerogel structures has appeared in high-impact journals and represents some of the most cited Chinese aerogel research internationally.

Zhejiang University — State Key Laboratory of Chemical Engineering

Zhejiang University, in Hangzhou, is a powerhouse for graphene aerogel and polymer aerogel research. The university's State Key Laboratory has produced numerous publications on 3D graphene aerogels with ultra-low densities, mechanically resilient aerogel composites, and aerogel-based electrodes for energy storage devices. Publications in Advanced Materials, Nature Communications, and ACS Nano have made Zhejiang University one of the most cited institutions in global aerogel literature.

Tongji University — College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Shanghai

Tongji University has built a significant body of research on aerogel-based building insulation, particularly silica aerogel blankets and panels integrated into energy-efficient building envelopes. The university collaborates with Chinese aerogel manufacturers, providing thermal performance data and application engineering that feeds directly into commercial product development.

Europe: From Building Physics to Particle Physics

Empa — Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology

Empa, based in Dübendorf near Zurich, is arguably Europe's leading aerogel research center for building applications. The laboratory has pioneered aerogel-based plasters and mortars designed for retrofitting historic buildings with minimal thickness penalty — a practical concern in European cities with strict preservation requirements. Empa also leads research on biopolymer aerogels from cellulose, alginate, and other renewable feedstocks, as well as supercritical CO₂ drying technology and scale-up.

Published in Energy and Buildings, Journal of Supercritical Fluids, and Materials, Empa's work is essential reading for anyone involved in aerogel-based building insulation or sustainable material development.

Fraunhofer Institute for Building Physics (IBP) — Bavaria, Germany

Fraunhofer IBP provides independent testing and characterization of aerogel insulation products, including blankets, boards, and rendering systems. The institute's building physics expertise — hygrothermal performance, fire behavior, long-term durability — makes it a trusted reference for manufacturers seeking European technical approvals (ETAs) and CE marking.

Fraunhofer IBP has tested products from major aerogel manufacturers and its Holzkirchen test facility is one of the most established in Europe for building envelope thermal performance evaluation.

CIC energiGUNE — Basque Country, Spain

CIC energiGUNE, located in Vitoria-Gasteiz, focuses on aerogels for thermal energy storage (TES) and battery thermal management. The center's research on aerogel-based phase change material (PCM) composites — where aerogel serves as a structural matrix for thermal storage media — is at the intersection of two fast-growing fields. For companies developing thermal management solutions for EV batteries or industrial energy storage, CIC energiGUNE's publications on hybrid aerogel-PCM systems are worth tracking.

CERN — European Organization for Nuclear Research

CERN's relationship with aerogel is unconventional but historically significant. Since the 1970s, CERN has driven development of high-optical-quality silica aerogel for use as Cherenkov radiators in particle detectors. Aerogel tiles in experiments such as LHCb (at CERN's Large Hadron Collider) and Belle II (at KEK in Japan) must meet extremely tight specifications for optical clarity, refractive index uniformity, and hydrophobicity. These requirements have pushed aerogel manufacturing capabilities well beyond what commercial insulation applications demand.

The aerogel for these detectors has been produced primarily by the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics (BINP) in Novosibirsk, Russia, which developed specialized large-format aerogel tiles with precisely controlled refractive indices. CERN's demand for multi-layer aerogel configurations has also driven innovations in bonding and optical matching techniques.

University Groups Advancing Aerogel Science

Beyond the major national labs and institutes, several university groups produce influential aerogel research:

  • University of Hamburg (Germany) — Prof. Irina Smirnova's group publishes extensively on supercritical drying processes, pharmaceutical aerogel formulations for drug delivery, and production scale-up. This group bridges fundamental heat and mass transfer science with industrial process design.
  • MIT (Cambridge, Massachusetts) — Multiple groups work on ultra-lightweight aerogel materials, aerogel-based electrodes for batteries and supercapacitors, and thermal insulation for extreme environments. Publications appear in Nature, Science, and Advanced Materials.
  • Tokyo Institute of Technology (Japan) — Research on transparent superhydrophobic silica aerogels and aerogel optical properties, connected in part to Japan's long history of supplying aerogel for particle physics applications at KEK.
  • Kyoto University (Japan) — Work on cellulose nanofiber aerogels, contributing to the growing field of bio-based aerogel materials from renewable feedstocks.
  • Northwestern University (Evanston, Illinois) — Research on polyurea cross-linked silica aerogels with improved mechanical toughness, addressing one of the fundamental limitations of silica aerogel for structural applications.

Why This Matters for Industry Professionals

Understanding the R&D landscape has practical value for several audiences:

For sourcing and procurement teams

Knowing which institutions are developing ambient-pressure drying, low-cost production methods, or new aerogel types helps anticipate where product costs and availability may shift. Collaborations between CAS institutes and Chinese manufacturers, for example, are directly linked to the expanding capacity of China's aerogel industry.

For product engineers

Published research from LLNL on 3D-printed aerogels, ORNL on carbon aerogel supercapacitor electrodes, or Empa on aerogel building plasters can inform material selection and specification. Many of these institutions make their findings publicly available through open-access publications and technical reports.

For business development and technology scouting

National labs in the US operate technology transfer programs. Fraunhofer institutes in Germany offer contract research. CAS institutes in China have formal technology licensing pathways. Identifying the right research partner can accelerate product development significantly.

Key Testing and Standards Resources

For companies that need independent validation of aerogel product performance, several institutions provide testing and standards services:

  • NIST (Gaithersburg, Maryland) — Develops reference methods for thermal conductivity measurement applicable to aerogel materials.
  • Fraunhofer IBP (Holzkirchen, Germany) — Building physics testing, hygrothermal performance, and certification support for aerogel insulation products seeking European technical approvals.
  • EU Notified Bodies — Various European conformity assessment bodies conduct fire safety, thermal performance, and durability testing on aerogel building products per EN standards.

Conclusion

The global aerogel R&D landscape is both broader and more accessible than many industry professionals realize. From NASA JPL's space heritage to Empa's building retrofits, from LLNL's 3D-printed aerogels to CERN's particle physics demands on optical quality, the research ecosystem is generating knowledge that directly feeds into commercial products and manufacturing processes.

For organizations serious about aerogel — whether as buyers, manufacturers, or application engineers — monitoring these institutions' publications and engaging with their technology transfer programs is a practical way to stay ahead of material and process developments that will shape the market in the coming years.

Selected Sources and Further Reading

  • NASA JPL — Stardust mission documentation and aerogel technical reports: jpl.nasa.gov
  • Oak Ridge National Laboratory — Carbon and graphene aerogel publications: ornl.gov
  • Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory — 3D-printed aerogel research: llnl.gov
  • Empa — Aerogel building insulation and biopolymer aerogel research: empa.ch
  • CIC energiGUNE — Aerogels for thermal energy storage: cicenergigune.com
  • CERN — Aerogel Cherenkov radiator development: home.cern
